I find myself consumed with indignation. Having attended pre-release screenings at this very location on previous occasions, I arrived for what proved to be an exercise in spectacular organizational failure. Following my customary practice, I appeared with time abundantly in hand. The queue, however, had been positioned outside—where the temperature hovered at one hundred and ten degrees, I should note—and it snaked around the theater's corner, doubled back past the elevators, continued beyond a stand of trees, and finally ascended the main entrance steps.

Well enough: those blessed with unemployment had apparently stationed themselves before the theater since early afternoon, forming their line at two o'clock for a seven o'clock screening. I reconciled myself to the possibility of rejection. Disappointing, perhaps, but hardly catastrophic. I elected to remain because I observed the steady arrival of additional hopefuls, none of whom were turned away by staff.

What follows, however, constitutes my gravest objection. The theater possessed a specific, predetermined number of tickets, ready for immediate distribution. They might have dispensed these with efficiency and released the remainder of us to our evenings. At minimum, they could have undertaken this simple courtesy after we had endured ninety minutes in that infernal line, once the crowd had diminished somewhat. The logic escapes me entirely. Fifteen tickets in hand? Count fifteen patrons and distribute accordingly. Why they held us there for no discernible purpose, offering no explanation at any juncture, remains an impenetrable mystery.

Three employees collected the passes we had printed at home—a completely superfluous operation. One distributed theater admissions while two young women simply stood about, perspiring. By seven o'clock, the line showed no sign of resolution, and we departed, concluding that some backstage catastrophe had thrown their schedule into disarray. My evening, needless to say, had been utterly squandered, and my patience along with it.

This is precisely the sort of establishment where one nurses pints while clad in tracksuit bottoms, on those particular afternoons when the effort of applying makeup seems an insurmountable task. Certainly no venue for white wine spritzers or cosmopolitans, it claims its chief virtue in economy. Under the banner of the Scream Pubs family, it offers drinks from a remarkable one pound eighty, and four or five pounds guarantees sufficient sustenance to send you home satisfied. Two pool tables occupy the space, though positioned with such unfortunate proximity that participants find themselves both wielding and receiving accidental jabs from errant cues every few minutes without fail. The downstairs section bristles with television screens broadcasting sporting events, yet the soundtrack proves so egregious that one immediately regrets not remaining home to watch the match in domestic comfort: the jukebox operates on a perverse algorithm, programmed to select the least-requested songs—those genuinely dreadful numbers no patron would ever pay to hear—thereby compelling desperate customers to insert coins and mercifully change the track for everyone's benefit.

Numerous other qualities conspire to discourage patronage. Its subterranean location condemns the place to darkness, dinginess, and an atmosphere of general despondency. This inherent gloom compounds with the evident fact that the premises have not witnessed refurbishment in an unconscionable span of years, creating that distinctive combination of dreary dimness blended with the shabby and the frankly grubby. The true nadir, however, awaits in the lavatories. Without wishing to appear excessively fastidious, I maintain modest requirements: namely, that toilets provide both tissue paper and functioning locks upon their doors. Yet after enduring an interminable queue for one of merely three facilities—of which one will invariably be marked out of order—one discovers these elementary provisions absent. By that point, having invested such considerable time waiting, resignation prevails and one simply tolerates these deficiencies, though the experience leaves an indelible impression of squalor that no bargain pricing can quite ameliorate.

After our sublime sojourn at Vdara's ESPA—that sanctuary of restful indulgence within the Mlife constellation—we resolved to embark upon a systematic exploration of sister properties, determined to sample each location at least once in our ongoing survey of therapeutic luxury. Since we had already taken up residence in the Grand that week, convenience and proximity dictated our next destination: the hotel's own spa, sparing us the trouble of venturing elsewhere through the glittering casino corridors. I telephoned that very afternoon, harboring modest hopes that they might accommodate us before our evening dinner reservations, which loomed only hours ahead. The receptionist who answered proved gracious and capable, managing somehow to secure us the final massage appointment of the day—a small victory against the tyranny of full booking calendars.

Regrettably, we arrived ten minutes behind our scheduled time, breathless and apologetic. In the unspoken protocols of massage etiquette, tardiness exacts its quiet penalty: those lost minutes vanish from one's treatment, never to be recovered, the sands already draining from an hourglass that began without you. After completing our check-in procedures and settling our accounts, we were conducted to separate changing facilities and assigned individual lockers. We dressed down hurriedly, acutely conscious that we had already squandered precious time.

Our massage therapist—a figure of professional calm—met us in the corridor and guided us to the treatment room designated for our couple's massage. The space itself possessed an understated loveliness: warm, dimly lit, conducive to that particular suspension of consciousness that bodywork requires. Both therapists proved exceptionally skilled, their hands moving with the confidence of long practice, though I confess their names have since escaped my memory. The session lasted less than fifty minutes, abbreviated not by any fault of theirs but by our own late arrival, that initial transgression echoing through the remainder of our visit. When they withdrew to allow us privacy for dressing, we discovered cold water waiting outside—a small, thoughtful gesture.

Afterward, my boyfriend and I separated to explore what remained of our access to the spa facilities. Though we were technically the final appointment, and closing time approached, the attendants never once betrayed impatience or hurried us along. Wandering through the various chambers, I mentally catalogued the amenities and compared them against Vdara's more generous offerings—particularly the provisions for post-treatment grooming. For the price commanded, I had anticipated something more expansive. Would I return? Certainly. Who among us can resist the temptation of such deliberate, delicious pampering?

How many chances does one extend to a restaurant merely because its location enchants or because local ownership tugs at one's loyalties? Everyone speaks reverently of the sticky buns, yet those belong to vanished days. Now one must request them explicitly—no longer do they arrive unbidden at your table, a small grace that once distinguished the place. Perhaps El Chorro finds itself unable to afford such gestures anymore, those minor extravagances that once composed its character.

The service provided by most of the female staff proves disappointingly inadequate. I say this as a woman myself, one who has worked in restaurants, whose family in Arizona owned establishments where attentiveness mattered. These servers seem incapable of independent thought, or perhaps management denies them the authority to exercise judgment. Consider what transpired on a recent evening: my friends had arrived before me, a party of eight ordering bottles of wine and food, assembled for happy hour though constrained by its limitations. Another friend and I arrived five minutes after happy hour concluded—we had been working—and my friend who hosted this gathering walked directly to the waitress as she approached our table, saying clearly, "These are the two ladies I mentioned." The waitress responded with swift pronouncement that happy hour had ended. I thought, here we go. I ordered a drink and appetizer, then appealed reasonably: "You see it's only five minutes after. Can't you check whether our drinks might still qualify? Our friends are ordering quite extensively." Her answer came flat and immovable: "I can't. Try asking the manager—perhaps he can bypass the system." She made no effort whatsoever. I could scarcely believe such inflexibility.

This incident followed another unfortunate experience. I had come to meet the same friend but arrived early on that earlier occasion, seating myself outside at the bar to wait. I ordered a cocktail. Two women sat to my right, another to my left. The women on my right requested the shrimp appetizer, only to be informed the kitchen had exhausted its supply during lunch service—would they please order something else? This occurred during happy hour's opening moments. The lady to my left then ordered the shrimp appetizer, though not from the happy hour menu. The shrimp materialized before her promptly. The other ladies and I noticed this contradiction immediately and questioned it. The female bartender who had declared them unavailable responded that they were out for happy hour specifically. We pressed: how did these differ? She insisted they came from different menus entirely. The explanation made no sense. I consulted my bartender, Tim, who summoned the manager. After hearing what had transpired, the manager approached both sets of ladies, apologized sincerely, and honored their original order. Yet the impression had already formed, adhesive and indelible in all our minds. I shared this account through my work network, reaching over six hundred local real estate agents. What misfortune for El Chorro that such incidents accumulate—lack of service, surprisingly consistent among female staff alone. Perhaps the male servers might yet rescue management from its foundering reputation.

The modest premiums that flash across advertisements invariably belong to term life insurance—a finite instrument, a policy with an expiration stamped into its very nature. Such coverage exists to shield families during those years when financial obligations press heaviest: one might purchase a twenty-year term designed to lapse precisely when children complete university or when the final mortgage payment clears, ensuring that an unexpected death neither derails education nor forces a widow into selling the family home. Should the policyholder survive to that appointed hour, however, the contract simply dissolves, yielding nothing. Consider the arithmetic: the typical buyer, somewhere in his thirties, secures protection extending into his fifties or sixties. Most reach that terminus alive. Only a small fraction perish prematurely, and their claims are funded, in essence, by the premiums paid by all those who do not.

The underlying mathematics prove straightforward. Imagine one hundred individuals, each purchasing coverage worth one hundred dollars and paying ten dollars annually. Should a single policyholder die, the insurer collects one thousand dollars total, disburses one hundred to the deceased's estate, and retains nine hundred. That surplus itself generates returns when invested prudently. Now multiply the participant pool while reducing the claim percentage further still: the potential profits expand enormously. Insurance companies, moreover, guard their risk pools with meticulous scrutiny, screening applicants to exclude those statistically predisposed toward claims. Life coverage becomes difficult or altogether unattainable for anyone harboring serious medical conditions; automobile policies grow costlier as driving records deteriorate.

Yet the enterprise should not be mistaken for charity. Actuaries calculate payouts with precision, weighing probability against exposure, incorporating term length and countless additional variables into their formulae. The insurance industry operates for profit, unambiguously so. Like the casino floor, where a single quarter fed into a slot machine might return thousands, the system functions on aggregate mathematics rather than individual fortune. The house, as always, maintains its edge—not through any particular transaction, but through the patient accumulation of probability across thousands of contracts, across decades, across the vast and predictable mortality of populations.
style_literary.coling::1c1fb589-36fc-45ac-bccc-1e9cced6: Picture Buffalo Wild Wings stripped of its wings—yes, and with marginally more beer, though only just. On a Thursday afternoon at four o'clock, three companions and I claimed an empty table in this establishment, a feat rendered shocking only by the venue's modest capacity, which surely accommodates fewer patrons than The Grind manages on its slowest evening. We settled ourselves and waited. Ten minutes elapsed—ten full minutes of studied neglect—before one friend, exasperated beyond endurance, rose to hunt down a waitress and request menus. Given that perhaps twenty-five employees circulated through the premises, locating someone to ask presented no difficulty whatsoever. What proved strange, disquieting even, was that not one of these abundantly available staff members had yet acknowledged our existence. The waitress provided no bottle list, though such a list apparently constitutes one of their prouder claims to distinction. Instead, we received a survey of their taps alongside a catalog of local eateries willing to deliver food to the bar. That particular innovation failed to enchant us. The tap selection itself disappointed thoroughly. A sprawling variety of overpriced local offerings dominated the board, supplemented by mediocre imports that inspired neither excitement nor curiosity. Colorado and Oregon certainly produce excellent beer, but mounting Dead Guy Ale on your tap hardly qualifies as daring or innovative. Not even a single sour graced the lineup. By this juncture our thirst had grown pronounced, our patience threadbare. Someone produced a phone and set a timer: fifteen minutes. If no server approached to solicit our order within that span, we would abandon the experiment entirely. A server did eventually materialize in our room. She attended immediately to the other party occupying the remaining tables. I leaned toward my companions and predicted, with grim certainty, that this woman would refuse us even the courtesy of eye contact—that she would settle the other table's bill, disregard our presence completely, and vanish. My prophecy fulfilled itself with depressing precision. She kept her back turned toward us throughout her entire visit to the room, as if we had achieved some remarkable state of invisibility. Departing, I stopped another server to inquire whether our room offered table service at all, or whether customers bore the responsibility of walking to the bar to order their own drinks. This second server, likewise avoiding my gaze, confirmed that yes, the room supposedly had service, then pivoted away to scrutinize her notepad with theatrical intensity. This location represents not their maiden venture. A company operating as many outlets as this one does should inaugurate new establishments with servers possessing basic competence in transporting one single product from point A to point B. Rude staff predominated—perhaps not universally, though I cannot say. After encountering three such specimens, I declined to risk meeting a fourth. The tap list proved uninspired. Superior selections await at Taste of Tops, Brat House, or intimate establishments like TMI. They serve no food; delivery arrangements hardly compensate. Ultimately, this remains big business masquerading as rebellion. The owners cultivate an image of edgy, tattooed, hip authenticity designed for cool kids, but the performance convinces no one paying attention.

The Sloan Digital Sky Survey has grown to encompass a region vast enough that galaxies dwelling in the sparse territories of cosmic voids can at last be detected and studied. Rojas and his collaborators have devised a technique capable of extracting more than a thousand void galaxies—those with density contrasts delta rho/rho falling below negative 0.6 on scales exceeding seven inverse-Megaparsecs—from the survey's accumulated data. In the present work, we set forth the luminosity function of these isolated systems and compare it against that of galaxies residing in denser cosmic neighborhoods.

Our measurement of the void galaxy luminosity function spans an absolute magnitude range from negative 21.5 to negative 14.5 in the r-band of the survey. We find that the void galaxy luminosity function admits a clean fit to the Schechter functional form, yielding characteristic parameters: a normalization Phi* of 0.19 plus or minus 0.04, multiplied by 0.01 h-cubed inverse-Megaparsecs cubed; a characteristic magnitude M_r* minus five times the logarithm of h equal to negative 19.74 plus or minus 0.11; and a faint-end slope alpha of negative 1.18 plus or minus 0.13. By contrast, the luminosity function of wall galaxies—those inhabiting filaments and sheets—exhibits a normalization of 1.42 plus or minus 0.03, in the same units; a brighter characteristic magnitude of negative 20.62 plus or minus 0.08; and a nearly identical faint-end slope of negative 1.19 plus or minus 0.07.

The fainter characteristic magnitude we observe corroborates the earlier findings of Rojas and colleagues, who reported that void galaxies appear intrinsically dimmer than their counterparts at higher densities. Yet the faint-end slope remains remarkably similar across environments. Further investigation of the luminosity function as a continuous function of density reveals that only wall galaxies in the very densest regions exhibit a shallower faint-end slope. Moreover, when we compare void galaxies to wall galaxies matched in physical properties—the bluest systems, those with Sersic indices below two, and those with H-alpha equivalent widths exceeding five Angstroms—the luminosity functions prove strikingly similar in shape, differing only in slightly brighter characteristic magnitudes. The observed faint-end slope of approximately negative 1.2 remains shallower than predictions from cold dark matter models, suggesting that voids are not, after all, teeming with unseen populations of dwarf galaxies.

What began as an interminable queue for frozen cocktails devolved, on a Friday evening in Queens, into violence so spectacular that witnesses would struggle afterward to render it coherent. The occasion was the unveiling of a Fat Tuesdays outpost within the Resort World Casino—a debut meant to summon celebration, not chaos. Instead, hundreds of patrons who had gathered in anticipation of iced daiquiris found themselves swept into something darker when tempers flared and the festive atmosphere curdled into rage.

The genesis of the melee, according to one casino employee, lay in a dispute between two women, each growing impatient as the line for alcohol stretched interminably before them. What might have remained a minor altercation metastasized when friends of both parties joined the fray, transforming personal grievance into collective pandemonium. By the time the confrontation reached its crescendo—around half past ten that night—guests were seizing whatever weapons lay at hand: chairs hoisted overhead, poles torn from their fixtures, anything that might serve as instrument in the escalating battle.

Security personnel converged on the scene, attempting with limited success to impose order upon the writhing mass of combatants. Bystanders, phones aloft, captured the bedlam and transmitted it instantly to social media, where footage revealed running skirmishes through the casino's corridors, profanity echoing off walls designed for more elegant pursuits. One witness, Elize Brown, described to local news the disorienting terror of the moment: chairs arcing through the air, chaos unfolding without pattern or predictability, each second pregnant with the possibility of fresh horror.

The toll was measurable in bodies and charges alike. Four security guards and one police officer sustained injuries requiring medical attention; ambulances clustered outside the casino as the night wore on. Three men faced consequences: Andrew Rivers and Jovan Bovell, both twenty-three years old, were charged with disorderly conduct, while Bovell received an additional charge for resisting arrest. Marcus Stewart, thirty, was issued two summonses for similar infractions. Several others departed in ambulances, their injuries demanding hospital care.

The casino, located near Kennedy Airport in the borough's sprawling precincts, issued a statement in the aftermath pledging enhanced security measures and closer collaboration with law enforcement to forestall any recurrence. A spokesman declared unequivocally that such behavior would find no tolerance within their establishment. The physical damage alone was estimated to exceed four thousand dollars—a figure that captured nothing of the evening's psychic cost, the way anticipation had curdled so swiftly into dread.

The truth, when examined without the distorting lens of internet hysteria, is that Canada stands neither vastly superior to the United States nor appreciably inferior. Were one to spend sufficient hours immersed in the pronouncements of rworldnews or rpolitics, one might arrive at the conviction that America has devolved into some manner of third-world police state, a dystopian landscape where liberty has perished and dignity lies trampled. The reality, however, is that the United States remains a fundamentally decent place to establish a life and pursue happiness.

To uproot one's entire existence, to abandon everything familiar and cherished, to begin afresh in a foreign country—this represents an ordeal of extraordinary magnitude. Such a rupture is not undertaken lightly, not unless one's present circumstances have truly become intolerable. Americans, by and large, do not perceive their lives as so desperately compromised that the immense effort required to emigrate appears justified. Moreover, developed nations like Canada do not simply fling open their borders to all comers; there exists instead a protracted and prohibitively expensive immigration process, one that winnows applicants with bureaucratic rigor.

Canada is, generally speaking, more expensive to inhabit than the United States. It is also considerably colder, a climate that does not suit all temperaments. Should a sudden wave of migrants appear at the Canadian border, the vast majority would likely struggle to secure employment—and what value do enlightened labor laws possess when one cannot find work at all?

Why, then, would mass immigration occur between these nations? There are no ground wars ravaging either country. The overwhelming majority of Americans and Canadians enjoy comfortable lives, raising their families in peace and security. Both are immense countries, sprawling across vast territories, yet they remain steadfast allies who do not persecute one another. The governments may differ in their particulars, but the societies themselves remain remarkably homogeneous in character. Furthermore, the Canadian dollar hovers at approximately seventy-six cents against its American counterpart. And Canada is cold—this bears repeating.

The notion that America constitutes a dystopia collapsing at the seams represents little more than hyperbolic nonsense, spouted by American teenagers who imagine themselves oppressed because they cannot afford the latest iPhone annually, and by European provocateurs. Life in the United States is not nearly as grim as embittered adolescents on Reddit would have one believe. It possesses its shortcomings, certainly, but every place harbors its particular troubles. For most people, overall, existence remains tolerably good, even decent, if never quite perfect.

I understand perfectly well that what follows will invite disapproval, but such is the nature of candor. On a Sunday afternoon, driven by genuine hunger, I ventured forth into the oppressive humidity of Scottsdale during monsoon season, searching for sustenance. After encountering several establishments shuttered for the Sabbath—each a small disappointment compounding the last—I resigned myself to visiting the reliably mediocre Schlotsky's Deli on Scottsdale Road. To my surprise, however, the landscape had shifted: gleaming new signage announced that Capriotti's and Everything Bagel had swept in to rescue the neighborhood from its culinary doldrums. A small victory, I thought—though I should have withheld my enthusiasm.

Upon entering, I was greeted not by cool air but by a stifling eighty-five degrees, the atmosphere thick and unpleasant. Approaching the register to place my order, I inquired of the heavily pregnant young woman—her face glistening with perspiration—how recently they had assumed control of the former Schlotsky's location. Her response was a theatrical rolling of the eyes, a downward glance, and the terse reply: two months, what would you like to order? I stated my preferences. She then requested my name for the order. I provided it. Another extravagant eye roll followed, accompanied by a shrug that conveyed, with remarkable eloquence, complete indifference. She announced that she could not spell. Now, I am typically unconcerned with whether strangers render my name correctly, and on this particular occasion I had even taken the precaution of pronouncing it phonetically, syllable by deliberate syllable. I dismissed the matter—until I happened to glance at the register screen facing me and observed her transcription: "corney." I laughed, perhaps unwisely. She bristled. "What?" she demanded. I explained that I was merely amused by her orthographic interpretation. She smirked, declared "it works," and turned away without further acknowledgment.

Proceeding to the pickup area, I observed the young man assembling my sandwich, his face streaming with sweat, which he periodically wiped away with the back of his wrist—an image both vivid and unfortunate. Meanwhile, another employee, evidently on break, hurtled past me at remarkable speed, clutching a plastic cup with questionable coordination, sliding dramatically to a halt before an empty table, where he flung himself down with theatrical exhaustion. One hoped his beverage contained no stimulants.

Listen: I recognize their youth. I acknowledge the brutal heat. I understand that one worker suffers from excessive energy, that the young woman endures pregnancy's discomforts, that she may harbor legitimate grievances about employment, existence, identity itself. Yet none of these circumstances absolves a fundamental truth: they sought positions in food service—an industry predicated upon serving others sustenance and civility alike. Courtesy forms part of service. Professionalism constitutes another. Where, I must ask, were the adults tasked with guiding these untrained youngsters, with teaching them to embody the establishment's standards?

The sandwich, I must note, was genuinely excellent. My gratitude to the perspiring tall fellow who prepared it.

In Palermo's storied dressing rooms, defender Roberto Vitiello speaks with the quiet desperation of a man who understands that his club's fortunes hang by the slenderest of threads. The Sicilian side, those islanders whose boots have wandered far from home without triumph, must reverse their wretched form on foreign soil, and they must begin this resurrection on Sunday, in Friuli, against Udinese. Not since the second of November—that crisp autumn day when they emerged victorious at the San Siro, dispatching AC Milan by two goals to none—have they collected three points beyond the familiar confines of their own stadium. Now, mired in the grey misery of three consecutive defeats, the most recent a 2-1 capitulation at home to those same Milanese visitors, Palermo find themselves languishing in eleventh position, urgency pressing upon them like the weight of Sicilian stone.

Vitiello, caught in conversation with the Italian press, his words measured yet tinged with anxiety, articulates what every supporter already knows in their bones. "We need to keep working hard in order to defend our Serie A status as soon as possible," he offers, the statement itself a kind of prayer. "We are disappointed not to have collected anything from our last three league games. But we must bounce back. Sunday's game at Udinese is important and we will give our all to clinch our second win on the road this season in Friuli."

Under Giuseppe Iachini's stewardship, Palermo have scraped together a paltry two points from their last six encounters—form that speaks not of ambition but of slow erosion. Their opponents sit two places lower in thirteenth, separated by the thinnest margin of a single point, themselves wounded after falling to bottom-dwelling Parma in midweek. In their own stadium, Udinese have become vulnerable, their fortress walls crumbling: four matches without victory, nine home fixtures yielding but a solitary win.

Andrea Stramaccioni, Udinese's beleaguered coach, spoke with the frankness of a man confronting uncomfortable truths. "Against Parma, we had the wrong approach to the game. My players underestimated Parma and we paid the price. We lacked determination and didn't take a shot on goal. Now we must turn the page immediately and show against Palermo the real Udinese."

Both sides arrive at this fixture diminished—Udinese without defender Ivan Piris and midfielder Giampiero Pinzi, suspended for the day; Palermo missing Edgar Barreto, sidelined three weeks with muscular damage. Yet there remains the young Argentine Paulo Dybala, Palermo's brightest flame with thirteen goals, who will lead the Rossaneri's attack with Franco Vazquez beside him, both men carrying their teammates' flickering hopes into Sunday's uncertain light.

Consider the notion that these services might actually be free. They are not, though the illusion persists. Both users—wherever they find themselves on the globe—require an internet connection to communicate. Even should you rely on complimentary wifi at your neighborhood café, that wifi exists to draw customers through the door, and someone, somewhere, absorbs the cost. What creates the appearance of freedom is the internet's inherent borderlessness, its indifference to geography. Traditional voice calls and text messages operate under entirely different constraints: your provider must compensate the provider in the distant country for the privilege of delivering your call or message across their infrastructure. The fees charged for this service are, more often than not, grotesquely inflated. The bottom line remains unchanged—you pay either way, merely through different channels and under different pretenses.

The telephone systems we inherit were constructed long ago, in an era when international communication commanded astronomical prices, and this historical reality established a precedent that endures. In those days, phone companies operated as national monopolies, frequently enjoying legal protection from any hint of competition. They could therefore impose exorbitant fees upon foreign telecoms attempting to route calls into their territory. They could do this precisely because no alternative existed, and because most people simply did not concern themselves with international calling costs. These fees functioned, in effect, as the cream skimmed off the top—the compensation telecom monopolies claimed for maintaining an affordable domestic calling infrastructure.

Then the internet arrived and transformed everything. Many internet service providers began as scrappy, competitive startups offering service over existing phone lines through dial-up connections. This origin made them eager to interconnect freely with content providers, since doing so enhanced their competitive position by improving service quality for customers. Even when separated by vast distances, they could secure inexpensive links by accessing "telecom hotels"—buildings where numerous companies competed to offer connections between cities, towns, and exchanges. Consequently, internet access has become remarkably cheap, while traditional phone providers have failed to adapt or keep pace.

This history should illuminate the ongoing debate over net neutrality. As the United States shifts toward monopolized infrastructure—you could once dial into any provider you wished, but most Americans now face only one or two high-speed cable options—internet service providers are attempting to revert to the old model, where they wielded considerably more power over consumer pricing. In countries with more open infrastructure, such as New Zealand, where you can select any fiber provider from among dozens in your local exchange, this remains far less pressing a concern.

The distinction is simple: you are already a phone company customer they hope to retain. Skype still hopes to make you one.

Embedded within section 51 of the Constitution of Australia, nestled among the enumerated powers of the Commonwealth, lies subclause (xxxi) — a provision that grants Parliament authority to legislate concerning the acquisition of property, while simultaneously imposing upon that power a crucial limitation: that all such acquisitions must proceed on just terms.

This constitutional clause is frequently invoked in abbreviated form as the 'just terms' provision, a shorthand that has entered the vocabulary of lawyers, scholars, and citizens alike. Beyond its considerable significance to the fields of Australian Constitutional Law and Property Law — domains where its influence reverberates through decades of judicial interpretation — the section has achieved a certain cultural prominence through its deployment as a plot device in The Castle, that quintessentially Australian film which has attained iconic status in the nation's cinematic imagination.

Text
Section 51(xxxi) reads as follows:

Jurisprudence
Though s51(xxxi) was drawn from the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution of the United States, the two provisions diverge in numerous and significant respects, each reflecting the distinct constitutional traditions from which it emerged.

The requirement of 'just terms' has been determined by judicial interpretation not to constrain the legislative powers of the State Parliaments, leaving them free from this particular federal constitutional restriction.

In the landmark decision of Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon articulated the fundamental purpose underlying the inclusion of this condition, stating that it existed "to prevent arbitrary exercises of the power at the expense of a State or a subject" — a formulation that would echo through subsequent jurisprudence.

The High Court of Australia's interpretation of the critical terms "acquisition" and "just terms" has had the practical effect, over time, of circumscribing the protection afforded to property rights under this constitutional guarantee. Moreover, the provision operates only when the Commonwealth engages in compulsory acquisition of property. Consequently, it functions as a contingent safeguard rather than as a general constitutional right or freedom enabling citizens to enjoy property rights unencumbered by governmental interference.

The Commonwealth may acquire property on just terms only for a "purpose in respect of which the Parliament has power to make laws" — a formulation that means every law supported by s 51(xxxi) must not derive its primary support from any other additional legislative power enumerated elsewhere in the Constitution.

Property
The High Court of Australia has adopted an expansive view of what constitutes "property" for constitutional purposes. Several members of the court seized the opportunity to examine the meaning of this term in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944). Justice Starke declared that the term encompasses "every species of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and choses in action." Justice McTiernan confirmed that the term property extends its reach to both tangible and intangible forms of proprietary interests.

The remarkable breadth of the concept of property within section 51(xxxi) receives vivid illustration in Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth, commonly known as the Bank Nationalisation Case. In that consequential litigation, Federal legislation contemplated the acquisition of private banks through the mechanism of vesting shares in those banks in the Commonwealth, with subsequent appointment of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon characterised these provisions as effectively removing meaningful control over the property of the private banks. He concluded that this constituted, in the essential sense, an acquisition of a proprietary right, even absent a simple transfer of title.

While statutory licences have occasionally been equated with proprietary interests in certain contexts, the removal of rights enjoyed under a statutory licence does not typically constitute an acquisition of property within the ambit of section 51(xxxi), given that licence conditions are inherently susceptible to legislative modification and regulatory change.

Acquisition
For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been acquired by somebody — a transfer must have occurred — and the acquisition must serve a Commonwealth purpose. This stands in marked contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the United States Constitution, where the ultimate destination of the property does not matter; it suffices that the holder of property has been deprived of it. Thus in JT International SA v Commonwealth the High Court determined that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which severely restricted the plaintiff's use of its trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth acquiring any property for itself. Similarly, in Cunningham v Commonwealth the High Court held that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold Pass privileges for retired members of Parliament did not constitute an acquisition of property within constitutional meaning.

In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Court determined that a grant to New South Wales which was tied to that State compulsorily acquiring property was invalid as an acquisition of property upon terms which could not be regarded as just. The validity of a grant in the absence of any requirement to acquire property was subsequently upheld in the later case of Pye v Renshaw.

Just terms
Typically, a determination of just terms calculated upon the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will prove sufficient to satisfy the constitutional requirement of just terms. Unlike the "just compensation" requirement embedded in the American Fifth Amendment, however, the phrase "just terms" imports no strict equivalence to market value. The arrangements offered must be "fair," or such that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair" in the circumstances. However, this judgment of "fairness" must take account of all the interests affected by the acquisition, not merely those of the dispossessed owner whose property has been taken.

The requirement of "just terms" does not necessarily mandate that a compensation package be presented as an integral part of the acquisition scheme itself. It is constitutionally sufficient that the scheme provides adequate procedures for determining fair compensation after the fact. However, the Court may scrutinise such procedures with considerable care to ensure their adequacy and fairness in practice.

There may exist certain acquisitions of property to which section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws supported exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution, which governs the territories.

Section 51(xxxi) represents an exception to the usual norm governing interpretation of the subsections of section 51 — namely, that one grant of power cannot be employed to "read down" or limit another. In this instance, however, the Court will not permit another grant of power to be construed so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation to the power granted by section 51(xxxi) itself.

Related legislation
The Deakin government's Lands Acquisition Act 1906, substantially drafted by Littleton Groom, was the first Commonwealth legislation to address the compulsory acquisition of land by the federal government. Its most contentious provision was a clause authorising the federal government to grant mining leases and regulate mining activities on Commonwealth land. Responsibility for administering compulsory acquisition was initially vested in the Department of Home Affairs.

The Chifley government's Darwin Lands Acquisition Act 1945 compulsorily acquired substantial tracts of land owned by Chinese-Australians in Darwin, precipitating the end of the local Chinatown that had flourished there. The legislation was first suggested in 1943 by the Northern Territory's administrator Aubrey Abbott, who proposed a combination of compulsory acquisition and conversion of the land to leasehold tenure in order to effect "the elimination of undesirable elements which Darwin has suffered from far too much in the past." He stated explicitly that he hoped to "entirely prevent the Chinese quarter forming again." He further observed with chilling directness that "if land is acquired from the former Chinese residents there is really no need for them to return as they have no other assets" in the region. The territory's civilian population had mostly been evacuated during the war, and the former Chinatown residents returned after hostilities ended only to discover their homes and businesses reduced to rubble and ash.

Having pursued the discussion that follows, I turned my attention to the authors' earlier work—the MUS-ROVER system upon which the present paper rests its foundations. This retrospective proved doubly illuminating: on one hand, it offered considerable aid in penetrating the current paper's arguments; on the other hand, it revealed itself as indispensable to any genuine comprehension of what the authors had attempted.

My estimation of this work, upon reflection, tends toward the favorable—I possess reasonable familiarity with the JSB chorales, with probabilistic frameworks, with n-gram methodologies and their cognates—yet I must confess that the paper presented formidable obstacles to understanding at numerous junctures. The proliferation of notation, rather than clarifying the exposition, obscured it.

The underlying ideas merit attention; the approaches demonstrate both originality and promise, worthy certainly of publication and of sustained investigation. Whether ICLR, in its present configuration, offers the appropriate venue for this particular paper remains, however, an open question. The difficulty lies neither in the application itself—musical applications can prove remarkably illuminating for broader computational questions—nor necessarily in the fundamental approach the authors have chosen. Rather, what I sense this work requires is the expansive canvas that only long-form journal publication can provide: sufficient space to elaborate these intricate ideas thoroughly, to furnish lucid running examples where the reader might otherwise stumble, to establish the necessary conceptual groundwork for the intended audience, to illuminate adequately the architecture of the predecessor system, perhaps even to demonstrate the approach's generality through application to a second dataset. The compressed format of a conference paper threatens to pack these elements too tightly, denying the project the detailed exposition it deserves. Were it feasible to isolate a single aspect of this system for concentrated attention, that might resolve the dilemma, though I confess I cannot envision precisely how one might accomplish such a distillation.

Substantial revision—though I hesitate to prescribe its exact contours within the mandated page limits—might warrant reconsideration of my evaluation. The authors' energies, I suspect, would find more productive employment in crafting an extended, more pellucid journal submission.

[Addendum: subsequent discussions and authorial revisions have prompted adjustment of my score]

Energy, we must understand, is not some ethereal substance that flows bodily through the void from one location to another. Rather, it exists as an inherent property of objects themselves, a characteristic that can undergo transformation into alternate manifestations through the performance of work upon those objects. Consider the familiar example: the energy harbored within your muscles undergoes conversion first into kinetic energy, then subsequently into potential energy possessed by the ball as you propel it upward along the slope of a hill. You "bestow" this energy upon the ball through the mechanism of work—which means, in the most fundamental sense, that you apply force across distance, your hand pressing against the sphere's surface as both move together through space.

To pursue this inquiry one step further: energy transfers itself according to the nature and constitution of the material through which it passes. A gas, for instance, might preserve energy within the vibrations oscillating between molecular bonds, then transmit that momentum—so to speak—into the motion of another gas particle, a phenomenon we recognize as thermal energy. A metal, by contrast, might conduct these vibrations across the regular geometry of its crystalline lattice. Certain perovskites emit electrical charges in response to shifts occurring at their constituent atomic sites when mechanical strain deforms their structure. In essence, energy manifests the inexorable progression from enthalpy—which is to say, order—toward entropy, or disorder, a transition dictated simply by the statistical probability that systems naturally evolve toward states of greater disorganization as time advances.

When you move a ball resting before you, you exercise your conscious intention, overcoming the stable equilibrium in which the sphere sits motionless. The chemical compounds within your arm demand that muscle fibers contract, which in turn propels your solid bones forward through space. The interaction between your solid arm and the ball produces this result: the ball absorbs energy into its chemical bonds, specifically the strong nuclear forces binding atoms together, which repel against the pressure of your hand advancing upon the sphere. Because the forces linking the ball to the table and the surrounding air prove weaker than the force of chemical energy concentrated in your arm, the ball rolls forward across the surface. Chemical energy itself derives from electron orbits seeking stable configurations, arrangements also governed by atomic forces throughout. Or, to simplify dramatically: energy represents anything possessing abundance, and when it contacts other things, it cannot help but distribute some portion of what it possesses among those things it touches.
style_literary.coling::1d5a005f-1162-4f21-a546-b8229951:
Here we encounter one of those perennial ironies: the injunction to "do as I say, not as I do." The United States, for better or worse, has cast itself in the role of global constabulary, thereby arrogating to itself the authority to prescribe the behavior of sovereign nations. Few would dispute the premise that unstable autocrats—men of volatile temperament and unchecked ambition—ought not to possess nuclear armaments; consequently, the international community tends to acquiesce, more or less tacitly, to American interventions.

But let us be precise: there exists no "acquiescence" in any meaningful sense. Events simply unfold. Other nations refrain from protest not from consent but from pragmatic calculation—their objections would accomplish little. They lack the leverage to impose sanctions of any consequence upon Washington, even were they so inclined. To address the broader question: the United States maintains its nuclear arsenal because it pioneered these weapons before any authority existed to prohibit their development. Once America had accumulated a substantial stockpile, the reality of its nuclear status became immutable, rendering further dispute futile.

Indeed, one might argue that American nuclear capacity has paradoxically limited proliferation. The United States extends its protective umbrella over numerous allies, obviating their need to pursue independent weapons programs. This arrangement, whatever its other implications, has likely resulted in fewer nuclear arsenals worldwide. It bears emphasizing that virtually every nation recognizes the imperative to constrain the development and deployment of nuclear, biological, and chemical weapons. America hardly stands alone in this conviction.

Thanks to the United Nations' nonproliferation treaty—and the classified protocols embedded within it—the United States retains authorization to supply nuclear weapons to select NATO partners. This same treaty, however, proscribes the creation and testing of such weapons under nearly all other circumstances. Because Washington operates within the treaty's provisions, and because the United States constitutes a pillar of UN peacekeeping operations, it assumes responsibility for censuring nations that pursue nuclear weapons programs and for deploying force when circumstances demand. The United Nations has, in effect, deputized America as global enforcer, though member states routinely lament that delegation of authority.

Consider the arithmetic of power: one country commands military resources exceeding those of all others combined. When that country undertakes an invasion you oppose, what recourse remains? You might resist openly, invite destruction, and perish. You might voice dissent, endure public humiliation, face ostracism, and sink into irrelevance. Or you might remain silent and accommodate yourself to circumstances. Thus far, all who have survived have chosen the third path—a testament not to justice but to the cold logic of disproportionate force.

Should a syllabus for the Biology course be available, examine it with care before attending the initial class meeting, absorbing its rules, its catalog of required materials, its calendar of obligations and deadlines. Return to this document habitually—indeed, each morning before class convenes—as a safeguard against oversight and forgetfulness. To impress the syllabus upon memory, employ the familiar arsenal of active reading: highlight passages in translucent color, underline phrases that demand attention, inscribe marginal annotations that translate the instructor's language into your own understanding.

The methods of engaging a syllabus are manifold and complementary. Underlining captures essential statements; highlighting bathes crucial information in chromatic emphasis; a hand-drawn star signals matter of particular importance; a carefully ruled box isolates key sentences or entire paragraphs from their surroundings; notes transcribed onto separate paper, or upon the verso of the syllabus itself, create a parallel text of your own devising. These techniques, applied judiciously, ensure that nothing vital escapes recollection. Before marking the original document, however, secure the instructor's permission—some educators prefer their syllabi remain pristine. Should you wish to preserve both an unmarked original and an annotated copy, employ a scanner to produce duplicates. This practice proves especially valuable should the syllabus undergo revision mid-semester, allowing fresh annotations on the duplicate while the original remains untouched.

Students lacking access to scanning equipment at home possess several alternatives. The nearest public library typically maintains scanning facilities, charging no more than twenty cents per page—a modest investment in academic preparation. Those who carry smartphones or tablets equipped with cameras may install applications designed specifically for document digitization. These programs transform photographed pages into PDF files, Word documents, and various other digital formats. Should neither option prove feasible, approach the school administration or the Biology instructor directly; they invariably welcome such requests and gladly provide assistance.

Most science courses, Biology among them, assess students a laboratory fee. This charge underwrites the materials required for experimental work—the slides and specimens, the chemicals and glassware that make empirical investigation possible. Instructors generally permit at least the first week of the term for payment. In most cases the fee proves refundable: upon successful completion of the course, the money returns to students' hands. Should a student damage equipment, however—whether through carelessness or misfortune—the fee typically remains forfeit. Handle all laboratory materials, hazardous and benign alike, with appropriate caution and respect.

Although not every instructor explicitly requires writing implements and paper for note-taking, their utility transcends formal requirement. Bring them regardless. The act of transcribing information aids retention; notes taken during class sessions become invaluable resources during subsequent review. To maximize the effectiveness of this practice, cultivate strong note-taking skills through deliberate study and application. Consult resources devoted to this essential academic craft for detailed guidance and methodology.

Before each class session begins, prepare your workspace by arranging necessary materials within easy reach—this simple ritual accelerates your readiness and prevents the awkward disruption of rummaging through your bag when the lesson has already commenced. Defer this preparation only if the instructor specifically requests that students leave materials untouched until given explicit permission. These moments before class also offer opportunity to review the previous day's homework and notes, confirming completeness and refreshing memory of recently acquired knowledge.

In the harsh glare of cell phone footage, a Virginia traffic stop has unraveled into something darker: a police officer beating and Tasering a seventeen-year-old boy, then allegedly attempting to erase the evidence of his own conduct. The video, grainy yet damning, has triggered an investigation — not merely into what transpired that January evening, but into whether an officer of the law tried to make the truth disappear.

Brandon Wyne sat in the backseat of his friend's vehicle, Courtney Griffith behind the wheel, when the blue lights flashed behind them on the tenth of January. The stated violation: a broken tail light, that minor mechanical failure that so often serves as pretext. Griffith, eighteen years old, pulled over. What followed would be captured in fragments of digital memory, preserved despite efforts to the contrary.

The officers approached. They claimed to detect the scent of marijuana drifting from the vehicle's interior — that familiar justification — and ordered its occupants to exit. Griffith refused, insisting she permitted no such substance in her car, demanding the production of an arrest warrant before she would comply. Wyne, aware of his status as a minor, agreed to emerge but imposed his own condition: no one would lay hands upon him until his mother arrived to witness whatever would unfold.

This resistance — modest, perhaps reasonable, certainly within the bounds of rights afforded even to the young — ignited an argument. Griffith's phone, propped upon the dashboard, recorded what came next. The officer's response was not negotiation but force: pepper spray discharged into the boy's face, chemical fire in his eyes. Then the Taser, its electrical charge convulsing through Wyne's body once, then twice. The footage captures his screams, his youth announced desperately: "I'm seventeen years old! Stop!"

Hands raised in surrender, the boy pleads — "Stop! Stop!" — but the officer's voice cuts through with a promise: "You're going to get it again." The threat becomes reality; the Taser fires once more.

The recording ceases when the officer discovers the phone, still witnessing from its perch. He seizes it, stops the documentation of his actions. Months would pass before Griffith discovered the footage lurking in her device's "Recently Deleted" folder — evidence nearly erased, almost lost.

Virginia Beach Police Chief Jim Cervera, reviewing what the lens preserved, offered careful words to the press: "There's some things I saw in that that I do not feel comfortable with." An investigation would examine not only the violence itself but whether tampering with evidence had occurred. The officer now occupies administrative duty, removed from the streets while questions multiply around what happened, what was recorded, and what someone tried to hide.

Judith Scott, born May 1, 1943, and departed from this world March 15, 2005, emerged as an American fiber sculptor of international renown despite—or perhaps through—the twin conditions that marked her existence from birth: Down Syndrome and deafness. Her enrollment in 1987 at Oakland's Creative Growth Art Center, an institution dedicated to supporting individuals with developmental disabilities, marked the beginning of a profound transformation. There, within those walls devoted to artistic possibility, Judith discovered not merely a passion or talent for abstract fiber art, but an entirely new language through which she could communicate with a world that had long remained closed to her. Her twin sister Joyce would later chronicle this remarkable life in Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott, published in 2016, a testament to sibling devotion and artistic revelation.

Judith entered the world in Cincinnati, Ohio, on that spring day in 1943, arriving alongside her fraternal twin Joyce into a middle-class family that already included older brothers. Unlike Joyce, Judith bore from birth the chromosomal distinction of Down Syndrome. During infancy, she contracted Scarlet Fever, an illness that ravaged her hearing and left her deaf—though this devastating loss would remain unrecognized, misunderstood, undiagnosed for years to come. The first seven and a half years of Judith Scott's life unfolded within the domestic sphere, surrounded by parents, her twin sister, and brothers. Though the developmental differences between the two girls grew increasingly apparent with each passing month, their parents made conscious, deliberate efforts to treat these youngest family members with equality, refusing to let disability dictate affection or opportunity.

Yet when the time arrived for formal schooling, the limitations of mid-century educational systems revealed themselves with cruel efficiency. Judith was deemed "ineducable." The single classroom designated for children with disabilities required passage of verbally-based entrance examinations—tests that Judith, her deafness still unrecognized, could not possibly navigate successfully. Following medical counsel, her parents made the agonizing decision to place Judith in the Columbus State Institution, formerly known as the Columbus State School, a facility for the mentally disabled. The date was October 18, 1950, and this separation carved wounds into both twins that would persist for decades.

The institutional records from Judith Scott's early years at the Columbus facility paint a portrait shaped by profound misunderstanding. Based upon oral testing conducted before anyone recognized her deafness, she was assigned an IQ of 30—a number that became a cage, denying her any training opportunities, any chance for growth or development. Stripped of her twin, that other half of herself, Judith descended into severe alienation. Behavioral difficulties emerged and proliferated. Her Clinical Record, written in the flat, detached language of institutional bureaucracy, notes: "She does not seem to be in good contact with her environment. She does not get along well with other children, is restless, eats messily, tears her clothing, and beats other children. Her presence on the ward is a disturbing influence." Subsequently, administrators transferred her to a smaller state institution in Gallipolis, Ohio, as though distance might solve what isolation had created.

Thirty-five years passed. Thirty-five years of complete separation, of sisterhood severed. Then, in 1985, following lengthy and extraordinarily difficult negotiations with state bureaucracies, Joyce Scott succeeded in becoming her sister's legal guardian. She brought Judith to California, a state whose laws guaranteed all mentally disabled citizens access to ongoing education, to continued learning, to possibility. Judith Scott would die of natural causes at her sister's home in Dutch Flat, California, a few weeks shy of her sixty-second birthday, having outlived her birth life expectancy by nearly half a century.

On April 1, 1987, Judith Scott crossed the threshold of the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the world's pioneering organizations providing dedicated studio space for artists with disabilities. For almost two years, she displayed little interest in artistic activity of any kind. Paint left her unmoved. She scribbled loops and circles, but her work contained no representational imagery, nothing that suggested engagement or vision. Her disinterest grew so pronounced that staff members seriously considered terminating her involvement with the program entirely.

Then came the breakthrough, arriving as such moments often do—casually, unexpectedly, without fanfare. Judith observed a fiber art class conducted by visiting artist Sylvia Seventy. Something in those materials, in that process, ignited recognition within her. Using whatever lay at hand, Judith spontaneously invented her own unique and radically different form of artistic expression. While other students stitched, she sculpted with unprecedented zeal and concentration, with an intensity that could not be ignored. Her creative gifts and absolute focus received immediate recognition, and she was granted complete freedom to select her own materials, to follow her vision wherever it led.

Taking whatever objects she found, regardless of ownership or conventional purpose, she would wrap them in carefully selected colored yarns, creating diverse sculptures of many different shapes and sizes. Some resemble cocoons or body parts, organic forms that speak to transformation and embodiment. Others rise as elongated totemic poles, vertical assertions of presence. Many works feature pairs—twin forms reflecting Scott's experience as a twin, that fundamental relationship severed for three and a half decades. Judith worked on her art five days weekly for eighteen years, an extraordinary sustained period of productivity that yielded over two hundred pieces in total.

Her first exhibition arrived in 1999, coinciding with publication of John MacGregor's book Metamorphosis: The Fiber Art of Judith Scott. Together, these events propelled her toward worldwide recognition, toward visibility long denied. Scott's work achieved immense popularity within the world of outsider art, and her pieces command substantial sums at auction and in galleries. She is now celebrated as a contemporary artist, no longer confined to the category of outsider, her work held in permanent collections at prestigious institutions: the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan, the American Visionary Art Museum in Baltimore, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Museum of American Folk Art in Manhattan, Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art in Chicago, Irish Museum of Modern Art in Dublin, The Oakland Museum, L'Aracine Musée D'Art Brut in Paris, Art Brut Connaissance & Diffusion Collection in Paris and Prague, and Collection de l'art brut in Lausanne, Switzerland.

Her exhibition history includes notable presentations: Judith Scott: Touchdown at Creative Growth Art Center in 2018, Bound and Unbound at Brooklyn Museum in 2014-15, retrospectives at Ricco Maresca Gallery in 2009 and 2002, and participation in the 57th Venice Biennale in 2017, among many others spanning continents and decades, testimony to an artist who found her voice through fiber, transformation, and wrapping the world in her vision.
